title: A simple application: under an hour, about eight approvals
prompt: If I ask the platform to build a very simple application, approximately how much effort and time should I expect?
summary: Measured on real deliveries: 20 to 45 minutes from the first prompt to a release you can open, of which your attention is a few minutes of reading and about eight clicks; the build itself takes under a minute.

items.label: Discovery
items.detail: 1 to 3 turns when the prompt is well formed; 2 to 5 default cards to accept

items.label: Four work products
items.detail: 4 next-step commands, 4 approvals; a few minutes of PL time each

items.label: Build
items.detail: 37 to 40 seconds measured; verification adds a browser run

items.label: Business Review + EAL
items.detail: 1 acceptance, 1 launch, first record in ten seconds

blocks.caption: Measured: 24 minutes from prompt to release for a mileage log once discovery converged.

rows.label: What counts as simple
rows.value: One entity, one or two roles, a worklist and a form, no integration: mileage log, contact directory, room reservation, visitor log.

rows.label: Your effort
rows.value: Write 3 to 6 sentences; read 6 cards; click accept about eight times.

rows.label: Model usage
rows.value: Roughly 16k to 28k tokens per turn; a session ceiling of 750k tokens covers a simple app comfortably.

rows.label: What slows it down
rows.value: Vague first prompts (discovery loops), authority wording such as I confirm the topology, asking PL to apply all defaults at once, and requesting changes at Build Plan instead of Requirements.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL to estimate a simple app
plPrompts.prompt: If I ask you to build a very simple single-entity application with two roles, what steps, approvals and time should I expect in this workspace? Do not build anything.

title: A moderately complex application: more discovery, more roles, a system of record
prompt: How would the development approach change for a moderately complex enterprise application?
summary: More discovery turns and a longer Blueprint; multi-role workflows with states and approvals; an integration-backed profile for a PostgreSQL system of record; architect review of the Solution Design; possibly several bounded applications instead of one.

rows: One core entity with a multi-step workflow; related records
Three to five roles with distinct visibility and approvals
Own schema plus a registered PostgreSQL system of record through the Integration plane
Architect reviews Solution Design; tester reviews qualification
Hours to a day, mostly discovery and review
One application, or two bounded ones sharing identity

blocks.text: Split by ownership, not by screen. Work Request and Work Order were delivered as one multi-role app; a procurement flow with a separate supplier audience is better as two applications with shared roles in UME.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL how it would approach a moderate app
plPrompts.prompt: How would the development approach change for a moderately complex enterprise application with several roles, a workflow and a PostgreSQL system of record? Do not build anything.

title: A highly complex application: decompose, integrate through governed connectors, phase the delivery
prompt: How would the platform handle a highly complex application involving multiple systems, integrations, APIs, databases, security requirements, and business processes?
summary: Decompose into bounded applications with shared identity; model the landscape in EKG; connect systems of record through the Integration plane (PostgreSQL and files today; enterprise connectors planned); phase delivery with an architect at each gate. Some of this is beyond today's connectors.

layers.title: Business processes
items: Discovered per process, each with actors and states

items.title: Map the landscape first
items.detail: Register the systems, interfaces and dependencies in EKG through Landscape Studio so placement and impact are grounded.

items.title: Decompose by ownership
items.detail: One application per bounded process with a clear data owner; shared roles published to UME; each app has its own schema and release lifecycle.

items.title: Connect systems of record through the Integration plane
items.detail: Register a binding, stage it, activate it; operations are pinned, policy-checked and receipted. Today only PostgreSQL and files; other connectors are on the roadmap.

items.title: Phase the delivery
items.detail: Deliver intake first, then approvals, then fulfilment; each phase has its own Business Review and can be rolled back.

items.title: Put an architect at every gate
items.detail: Solution Design review per application; landscape confirmation per phase; security requirements written into Requirements so they become tests.

blocks.title: Honest limits today
blocks.text: Applications are single-entity per generation; multi-entity domains are delivered as several apps. Enterprise SaaS and ERP connectors, transformation mapping and production environments are planned work. A highly complex program today is a sequence of bounded PL deliveries plus integration through PostgreSQL.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL how it would handle a complex program
plPrompts.prompt: How would you handle a highly complex application involving multiple systems, integrations, APIs, databases, security requirements and business processes? Be explicit about what this workspace supports today. Do not build anything.

title: What makes an application simple, medium, complex or enterprise-scale
prompt: What factors determine whether an application is considered simple, medium, complex, or enterprise-scale?
summary: Number of entities and relationships, workflow states and roles, systems of record and integrations, data migration, security and compliance requirements, environments, and whether an existing application constrains the design.

blocks.caption: Effort grows with integrations and roles more than with screens.

blocks.text: Ask PL for a discovery-only assessment first: it will name the actors, states and systems it sees and you can judge the size before committing.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL to size an idea
plPrompts.prompt: Assess the complexity of this idea before building anything: name the entities, roles, workflow states, integrations and security needs you see, and say whether it is simple, medium or complex. Do not build anything.

title: Three examples: mileage log, work management, procurement across systems
prompt: Can you give me an example of a simple application, a moderately complex application, and a highly complex application that could be built using this platform?
summary: Simple: Mileage Reimbursement Log. Moderate: Work Management with work requests and work orders across roles. Complex: procurement across intake, approvals, supplier records and finance, delivered as several bounded applications with governed integrations.

rows: Form + worklist; submitter and manager; amount = miles x rate rounded half-up
One app, own schema, roles in UME, 14 tests, browser evidence
Work request to work order; requester, dispatcher, technician, manager; states and approvals
One multi-role app with record authorization and audit
Intake queue with owners and statuses; records in a PostgreSQL system of record
Integration-backed app through the Integration plane
Purchase requisition, approvals by threshold, supplier onboarding, finance posting
Three or four bounded apps, shared roles, PostgreSQL connectors; ERP posting planned

plPrompts.label: Ask PL for examples it can build
plPrompts.prompt: Give me an example of a simple, a moderately complex and a highly complex application that could be built with the capabilities installed in this workspace, and say what would be needed for each. Do not build anything.

title: How the process differs for each example
prompt: For each of those examples, explain how the development process would differ.
summary: The lifecycle is the same; what changes is the number of discovery turns, the depth of design review, the landscape binding, the qualification campaigns and whether the delivery is one application or a phased set.

rows: Several turns: roles, states, who sees what, escalation
Per process; systems and owners mapped first
Integration bindings per system of record
Architect per app; security requirements as tests
